title: Sharps safety & inoculation injuries
blurb: What counts as a sharp, safe handling and sharps bins, the 2013 Sharps Regulations, and exactly what to do after a needlestick or splash.
question: While clearing the bracket table after an extraction, you catch your finger on a used local anaesthetic needle that was left uncapped. The patient has just left the building. What do you do in the next few minutes, who do you tell, and what should the practice change so it doesn't happen again?

teach.body: An inoculation injury happens when a patient's blood or saliva gets into your body through the skin (a needlestick or cut) or onto your eyes, nose or mouth (a splash). It can pass on blood-borne viruses: hepatitis B, hepatitis C and HIV. Gloves do not stop a needle, so prevention depends on how you handle, pass and dispose of every sharp. Most sharps injuries are preventable, and many happen when people are rushing or clearing up.

teach.caption: The Health and Safety (Sharp Instruments in Healthcare) Regulations 2013. Employees must report any sharps injury to their employer as soon as possible.

teach.body: The person who uses a sharp disposes of it, straight away, at the point of use. Never carry an uncovered needle across the surgery and never leave one on the tray for someone else to find. Don't recap by hand: if a needle must be resheathed between injections, use a one-handed scoop or a recapping device. Pass sharp instruments through an agreed neutral zone, not hand to hand. Put used endodontic files in a puncture-resistant holder until they are disposed of.

teach.body: Treatment after exposure, such as post-exposure prophylaxis (PEP) for HIV, works best when started as soon as possible, so report the injury straight away, not at the end of the session. Your hepatitis B status is checked too. The employer reports the injury under RIDDOR when required, for example if the source is known to carry a blood-borne virus. Near misses also get reported: a scalpel dropped on the floor or a needle found in a domestic waste bag. Recording every incident helps the practice spot patterns and stop repeats.

teach.text: Never suck or scrub the wound, and never wait until the end of the day to report it. The order is: encourage bleeding, wash, cover, report, occupational health.

summary: You can now recognise every type of dental sharp, handle and dispose of sharps safely, explain what the Sharps Regulations 2013 require, and give the correct first aid and reporting steps after a needlestick or splash injury.

A.q: A dental nurse has a needlestick injury from a used local anaesthetic needle. What is the immediate first aid?
options: Suck the wound, then apply antiseptic
Scrub the area hard with a nailbrush
Cover it and finish the procedure
Encourage bleeding and wash with soap
A.why: Gently encourage bleeding, then wash with soap and warm running water and cover with a waterproof plaster.

whyNot.0: Sucking the wound puts blood in your mouth, another portal of entry.
whyNot.1: Scrubbing damages the skin and can help micro-organisms enter.
whyNot.2: The wound must be washed and the injury reported straight away.

A.q: During surgery turnover, who is responsible for disposing of a used sharp?
options: The practice manager
The person who used it
Whoever cleans the surgery
The decontamination lead
A.why: The user of the sharp is responsible for disposing of it immediately at the point of use.

whyNot.0: The manager sets the policy but doesn't dispose of each sharp.
whyNot.2: Leaving sharps for someone else to clear causes injuries.
whyNot.3: Sharps should never reach decontamination with the instruments.

A.q: A sharps container has reached its fill line. What should you do?
options: Seal it and replace it
Press the contents down
Empty it into a yellow bag
Use it until it is full
A.why: Once the fill line is reached, the container is sealed, labelled and replaced.

whyNot.1: Pushing contents down risks a sharps injury.
whyNot.2: Sharps must never be emptied into bags; they would pierce them.
whyNot.3: Overfilling means sharps can stick out or fall out of the opening.

B.q: Which of these should NOT routinely go into a sharps container?
options: A matrix band
A broken LA cartridge
Paper instrument packaging
A used endodontic file
B.why: Paper packaging isn't sharp, so it goes in the correct non-sharps waste stream.

whyNot.0: Matrix bands have sharp edges and are treated as sharps.
whyNot.1: Broken cartridges are sharp glass contaminated with medicine.
whyNot.3: Used endodontic files are sharp and go in the sharps bin.

B.q: A needle must be resheathed because the dentist will give a second injection to the same patient shortly. What is the safest method?
options: A one-handed scoop or recapping device
Two-handed recapping, very carefully
Ask the nurse to hold the cap
Leave it uncapped on the bracket table
B.why: If recapping can't be avoided, use a one-handed scoop or recapping device so your hand never goes near the needle tip.

whyNot.1: Two-handed recapping is a leading cause of needlestick injuries.
whyNot.2: Holding the cap for someone else puts your hand directly in the path of the needle.
whyNot.3: An uncapped needle left on the tray is a hazard to everyone.

B.q: A sharps bin is standing on the floor in a busy surgery walkway. What is the best action?
options: Leave it where it is easy to reach
Put it in a cupboard under the sink
Cover it with a paper towel
Fix it securely at a suitable height
B.why: Sharps bins must be secure, stable and at a suitable height close to where sharps are used.

whyNot.0: A bin on the floor can be kicked over or reached by children.
whyNot.1: A cupboard puts the bin away from the point of use and in a splash zone.
whyNot.2: Covering it doesn't make it stable and blocks the opening.

C.q: A colleague says she is protected against needlestick injuries because she wears gloves. What is the best response?
options: Gloves are puncture-proof
Needles go straight through gloves
Wearing two pairs of gloves makes it safe
Nitrile gloves stop any sharp
C.why: Gloves reduce contamination but a needle passes straight through them, so safe handling is still essential.

whyNot.2: Double gloving may reduce the blood transferred, but a needle still goes through.
whyNot.3: No examination glove material stops a needle.

C.q: A scalpel slips off the tray and falls to the floor, but nobody is hurt. What should happen?
options: Nothing, as no one was injured
Pick it up and reuse it
Report it as a near miss
Mention it at your next appraisal
C.why: Near misses are reported under local policy so the practice can learn and prevent a future injury.

whyNot.0: Near misses are reported precisely so they don't become injuries.
whyNot.1: A dropped scalpel is contaminated and goes straight in the sharps bin.
whyNot.3: Incidents are reported promptly, not saved up for an appraisal.

C.q: After first aid and reporting a needlestick injury, why should occupational health be contacted urgently?
options: Treatment like PEP works best early
To arrange a replacement sharps container
To book the next staff meeting
To check the needle was in date
C.why: Post-exposure treatment, such as PEP for HIV, is most effective when it is started as soon as possible.

whyNot.1: Replacing bins doesn't need occupational health.
whyNot.2: Staff meetings may review incidents later, but this isn't urgent care.
whyNot.3: The needle's expiry date is irrelevant to the injured person's treatment.

reteach.title: Treat every sharp like a lit match
reteach.question: You'd never pass a lit match from hand to hand or carry it across a room. How does that help you handle dental sharps?

blocks.h: Put it out where you are
blocks.body: With a lit match, you put it out yourself, straight away, right where you are. You don't hand it on, wander off with it, or try to cover it back up with your fingers. Treat used sharps the same: the person who used it disposes of it, immediately, in a bin right next to the chair. And if you do get burned, you act at once: first aid first, then tell someone straight away so they can help.

blocks.text: Gloves don't stop needles. Your protection is safe handling, safer sharps and a bin at the point of use.

explain.body: Needles, cartridges, blades, burs, files, matrix bands, wires and broken glass are all sharps. The user disposes of them at the point of use, never recaps by hand and passes instruments through a neutral zone.

test.q: Which item should be treated as a sharp when clearing the bracket table?
options: Cotton wool roll
Used saliva ejector
Patient bib
Matrix band
test.why: Matrix bands have thin, sharp edges and go in the sharps container.

whyNot.0: Cotton wool rolls are soft clinical waste.
whyNot.1: Saliva ejectors are plastic and not sharp.
whyNot.2: A patient bib is not sharp.

explain.body: Assembled correctly, secured at a suitable height near the chair, temporary closure used, never pushed down, sealed at the fill line. Lid colour shows the waste stream.

test.q: Which sharps bin lid colour is used for sharps contaminated with medicines, such as used LA cartridges?
options: Purple
Yellow
Black
Blue
test.why: Yellow-lidded sharps bins take sharps contaminated with medicines, such as used local anaesthetic cartridges.

whyNot.0: Purple lids are for cytotoxic and cytostatic contamination.
whyNot.2: Black is the domestic waste colour, never used for sharps.
whyNot.3: Blue-lidded containers are for unwanted medicines, not used sharps.

explain.body: Encourage bleeding gently, wash with soap and warm running water, and cover with a waterproof plaster. Don't suck or scrub. For a splash to the eyes or mouth, rinse with plenty of water and don't swallow.

test.q: A nurse's eye is splashed with a patient's saliva during treatment. What should she do first?
options: Rub the eye with a tissue
Wait to see if it turns red
Rinse with plenty of water
Apply antiseptic eye drops
test.why: A splash to the eye is irrigated straight away with plenty of water, then reported like any inoculation injury.

whyNot.0: Rubbing can work contamination in and damage the eye.
whyNot.1: Waiting delays first aid and reporting.
whyNot.3: Antiseptic is not used in the eye; water is.

explain.body: The Sharps Regulations 2013 require employers to avoid unnecessary sharps, use safer sharps, stop recapping, place bins near use, train staff and provide treatment. Employees must report injuries promptly. Near misses are reported too.

head: Who
Duty
rows: Safer sharps, bins near use, training, treatment

test.q: Under the Sharps Regulations 2013, what must an employee do after a sharps injury?
options: Report it to the employer promptly
Report it to the GDC
Wait until the end of the week
Tell only the source patient
test.why: Employees must tell their employer about a sharps injury as soon as practicable so it can be assessed and treated.

whyNot.1: The GDC regulates professionals; it isn't where injuries are reported.
whyNot.2: Delay reduces the benefit of any treatment.
whyNot.3: The injury is reported to the employer; the dentist then talks to the patient.
